text: We design single-shot shaped pulses for ultra-high-fidelity population transfer in a three-level quantum system with a lambda configuration. The aim is to achieve reliable transfer while suppressing unwanted occupation of the intermediate state and reducing sensitivity to control errors. High fidelity is guaranteed through the Lewis–Riesenfeld method, which generates a family of exact-transfer solutions. Each solution evolves along a single dynamical mode of the corresponding invariant, providing analytical control over the process rather than relying entirely on numerical pulse optimization. Within this family, we identify a one-parameter tracking solution that jointly regulates transfer fidelity, excited-state occupation, and robustness. The parameter makes the trade-offs among these three experimentally important quantities explicit. Robustness is measured by the minimum percentage change in pulse area required to raise the infidelity above $10^{-4}$. At moderate pulse areas, the proposed shapes are more robust than both Gaussian pulses and adiabatically optimized alternatives. The results show that exact invariant-based control can offer practical advantages without requiring excessively large pulse resources.

text: To think about the future of money, consider the Yapese, a Micronesian culture in the early twentieth century. Their currency demonstrates that money does not have to be portable, physically exchanged, or even immediately accessible in order to function. The Yapese use large limestone disks known as Rai stones. Some are enormous—the largest weighs roughly four tons and measures twelve feet across—so moving them for every transaction would be impossible. Instead, ownership is maintained through collective knowledge. The community agrees on who owns each stone, or a share of it, even when the object itself remains in the same place. One well-known story describes sailors transporting a Rai stone across the ocean when it fell overboard. The stone could no longer be seen or recovered, yet the community continued to recognize both its existence and its owner because everyone accepted the account of what had happened. The stone’s monetary value therefore rested not on physical possession, but on shared belief and an agreed record of ownership.
